claim: SARS-CoV-2 infects cells through binding to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2).
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infects cells through binding to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2 is mediated by the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the viral spike (S) glycoprotein.
source: This interaction is mediated by the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the viral spike (S) glycoprotein.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: The spike protein can adopt multiple conformations, which controls the exposure of the ACE2-binding site in the RBD.
source: Structural and dynamic data have shown that S can adopt multiple conformations, which controls the exposure of the ACE2-binding site in the RBD.
evidence: This is supported by structural and dynamic data referenced in the manuscript.

claim: D614G modulates the energetics of the RBD position in a manner similar to ACE2 binding.
source: We find that D614G modulates the energetics of the RBD position in a manner similar to ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antibodies that target diverse epitopes, including those distal to the RBD, stabilize the RBD in a position competent for ACE2 binding.
source: We also find that antibodies that target diverse epitopes, including those distal to the RBD, stabilize the RBD in a position competent for ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments and FCS assays.

claim: Antibody binding mediates enhancement of ACE2 binding.
source: Parallel solution-based binding experiments using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) indicate antibody-mediated enhancement of ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is supported by FCS experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the etiologic agent of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the etiologic agent of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (Zhou et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 binds the cell receptor ACE2 through its envelope glycoprotein spike (S), which subsequently promotes membrane fusion and cell entry.
source: To infect host cells, SARS-CoV-2 binds the cell receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) through its envelope glycoprotein spike (S), which subsequently promotes membrane fusion and cell entry (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Letko et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020; ; Wang et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and established knowledge.

claim: S is a trimer of heterodimers, with each protomer consisting of S1 and S2 subunits.
source: S is a trimer of heterodimers, with each protomer consisting of S1 and S2 subunits (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1.

claim: S1 contains the receptor-binding domain (RBD), which includes the ACE2 receptor-binding motif (RBM).
source: S1 contains the receptor-binding domain (RBD), which includes the ACE2 receptor-binding motif (RBM).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: S2 forms the spike stalk and undergoes a large-scale refolding during promotion of membrane fusion.
source: S2, which forms the spike stalk, undergoes a large-scale refolding during promotion of membrane fusion (Cai et al., 2020; Tortorici and Veesler, 2019; Walls et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Structures of the soluble trimeric ectodomain of the SARS-CoV-2 S glycoprotein in two prefusion conformations have been reported.
source: Structures of the soluble trimeric ectodomain of the SARS-CoV-2 S glycoprotein in two prefusion conformations have been reported (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The RBD of each protomer can independently adopt either a 'down' (closed) or an 'up' (open) position, giving rise to asymmetric trimer configurations.
source: These distinct conformations demonstrate that the RBD of each protomer can independently adopt either a 'down' (closed) or an 'up' (open) position, giving rise to asymmetric trimer configurations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 1A.

claim: The RBM is occluded in the down conformation.
source: The RBM is occluded in the down conformation, suggesting that the RBD must transition to the up conformation to bind ACE2.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: The RBD must transition to the up conformation to bind ACE2.
source: The RBM is occluded in the down conformation, suggesting that the RBD must transition to the up conformation to bind ACE2.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations.

claim: Structures of S bound to ACE2 show the RBD in the up conformation.
source: Indeed, structures of S bound to ACE2 show the RBD in the up conformation (Zhou et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural data.

claim: Structural data were corroborated by real-time analysis of the conformational dynamics of S through single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) imaging.
source: Structural data were corroborated by real-time analysis of the conformational dynamics of S through single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) imaging (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous smFRET studies.

claim: The D614G variant (B.1 lineage) had supplanted the ancestral virus (strain Wuhan-1) worldwide by the summer of 2020.
source: By the summer of 2020, the SARS-CoV-2 S variant D614G (B.1 lineage) had supplanted the ancestral virus (strain Wuhan-1) worldwide, and structural analysis showed that D614G disrupts an interprotomer contact (Zhang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation and established knowledge.

claim: D614G disrupts an interprotomer contact.
source: By the summer of 2020, the SARS-CoV-2 S variant D614G (B.1 lineage) had supplanted the ancestral virus (strain Wuhan-1) worldwide, and structural analysis showed that D614G disrupts an interprotomer contact (Zhang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural analysis.

claim: D614G results in a shift in the RBD conformation toward the up position, which is competent for ACE2 binding.
source: This disruption results in a shift in the RBD conformation toward the up position, which is competent for ACE2 binding, consistent with increases in in vitro virus-cell binding mediated by ACE2 and infectivity (Korber and Fischer, 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: D614G is consistent with increases in in vitro virus-cell binding mediated by ACE2 and infectivity.
source: This disruption results in a shift in the RBD conformation toward the up position, which is competent for ACE2 binding, consistent with increases in in vitro virus-cell binding mediated by ACE2 and infectivity (Korber and Fischer, 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The enhanced exposure of the RBM in the D614G variant led to increased sensitivity to neutralizing antibodies.
source: At the same time, the enhanced exposure of the RBM in the D614G variant led to increased sensitivity to neutralizing antibodies (Weissman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The RBD showed stabilization in the up position, as well as an intermediate conformation, upon treatment with a neutralizing S2 stalk-directed antibody.
source: Furthermore, the RBD showed stabilization in the up position, as well as an intermediate conformation, upon treatment with a neutralizing S2 stalk-directed antibody (Li et al., 2022a; Ullah et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ACE2 binding is controlled by the conformational dynamics of the RBD.
source: Our results indicate that ACE2 binding is controlled by the conformational dynamics of the RBD, with ACE2 capturing the intrinsically accessible up conformation rather than inducing a conformational change.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments.

claim: ACE2 captures the intrinsically accessible up conformation rather than inducing a conformational change.
source: Our results indicate that ACE2 binding is controlled by the conformational dynamics of the RBD, with ACE2 capturing the intrinsically accessible up conformation rather than inducing a conformational change.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments.

claim: Antibodies that target diverse epitopes—including epitopes in the NTD and in the S2 stalk, which are distal to the RBD—tend to shift the RBD equilibrium on the D614 spike toward the up conformation, enhancing ACE2 binding.
source: We find that antibodies that target diverse epitopes—including epitopes in the N-terminal domain (NTD) and in the S2 stalk, which are distal to the RBD—tend to shift the RBD equilibrium on the D614 spike toward the up conformation, enhancing ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET and FCS experiments.

claim: The D614G spike existed in an equilibrium where the RBD favors the up conformation prior to antibody binding.
source: The D614G spike existed in an equilibrium where the RBD favors the up conformation prior to antibody binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments.

claim: Antibodies that target the S2 stalk further promoted the RBD-up conformation on the D614G spike.
source: Nonetheless, antibodies that target the S2 stalk further promoted the RBD-up conformation on the D614G spike.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the smFRET experiments.

claim: Long-range allosteric modulation of the RBD equilibrium regulates exposure of the ACE2-binding site.
source: We thus observe long-range allosteric modulation of the RBD equilibrium, which in turn regulates exposure of the ACE2-binding site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A4-tagged SΔTM homo-trimers maintained more than 50% of antibody binding compared to untagged SΔTM.
source: A4-tagged SΔTM homo-trimers maintained more than 50% of antibody binding compared to untagged SΔTM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with MAb362-IgG1 and 4A8 showing no statistically significant loss of binding.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MAb362-IgG1 and 4A8 showed no statistically significant loss of binding to A4-tagged SΔTM compared to untagged SΔTM.
source: A4-tagged SΔTM homo-trimers maintained more than 50% of antibody binding compared to untagged SΔTM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with MAb362-IgG1 and 4A8 showing no statistically significant loss of binding.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Double 161/345 A4-labeled SΔTM trimers maintain native functionality during ACE2 binding and near-native antigenic properties.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that double 161/345 A4-labeled SΔTM trimers maintain native functionality during ACE2 binding and near-native antigenic properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FCS and ELISA data.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for ACE2 binding to untagged SΔTM is approximately 12.4 ± 2.7 nM.
source: FCS experiments allowed us to calculate dissociation constants (KD) for ACE2 binding to untagged and A4-tagged SΔTM proteins in solution (Figure 2C), which were approximately 12.4 ± 2.7 and 8.3 ± 1.2 nM, respectively, in rough agreement with values obtained through surface-based assays (Walls et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is determined from FCS experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for ACE2 binding to A4-tagged SΔTM is approximately 8.3 ± 1.2 nM.
source: FCS experiments allowed us to calculate dissociation constants (KD) for ACE2 binding to untagged and A4-tagged SΔTM proteins in solution (Figure 2C), which were approximately 12.4 ± 2.7 and 8.3 ± 1.2 nM, respectively, in rough agreement with values obtained through surface-based assays (Walls et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is determined from FCS experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: smFRET trajectories acquired from individual unbound SΔTM D614 molecules showed transitions between high (~0.65) and low (~0.35) FRET states, suggestive of the down and up RBD positions, respectively.
source: smFRET trajectories acquired from individual unbound SΔTM D614 molecules showed transitions between high (~0.65) and low (~0.35) FRET states, suggestive of the down and up RBD positions, respectively (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is observed in smFRET data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: A kinetic model with two non-zero FRET states, and a 0-FRET state corresponding to photobleaching, was sufficient to describe the dynamics observed in the smFRET trajectories.
source: Hidden Markov modeling (HMM) confirmed that a kinetic model with two non-zero FRET states, and a 0-FRET state corresponding to photobleaching, was sufficient to describe the dynamics observed in the smFRET trajectories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by HMM analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SΔTM D614 shows 60% ± 3% occupancy in the high-FRET state and 40% ± 3% occupancy in the low-FRET state.
source: Consistent with SΔTM D614 preferring the down conformation, HMM analysis indicated 60% ± 3% occupancy in the high-FRET state and 40% ± 3% occupancy in the low-FRET state (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After incubation with ACE2, SΔTM D614 shows 34% ± 3% in the high-FRET state and 66% ± 3% occupancy in the low-FRET state.
source: The same FRET states were detected after incubation with ACE2, but the conformational equilibrium shifted to 34% ± 3% in the high-FRET state and 66% ± 3% occupancy in the low-FRET state (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: ACE2 promotes the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614.
source: This result is consistent with ACE2 promoting the RBD-up conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the shift in FRET state occupancies upon ACE2 binding.

claim: For SΔTM D614, transition from the RBD-down to the RBD-up conformation occurred at kup = 2.6 ± 0.2 s–1.
source: This analysis indicated that transition from the RBD-down (high FRET) to the RBD-up (low FRET) conformation occurred at kup = 2.6 ± 0.2 s–1, whereas the RBD-up to RBD-down transition occurred at kdown = 3.8 ± 0.2 s–1.
evidence: This is determined from maximum likelihood optimization of the kinetic model.

claim: For SΔTM D614, the RBD-up to RBD-down transition occurred at kdown = 3.8 ± 0.2 s–1.
source: This analysis indicated that transition from the RBD-down (high FRET) to the RBD-up (low FRET) conformation occurred at kup = 2.6 ± 0.2 s–1, whereas the RBD-up to RBD-down transition occurred at kdown = 3.8 ± 0.2 s–1.
evidence: This is determined from maximum likelihood optimization of the kinetic model.

claim: ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the RBD-down to the RBD-up transition (kup = 2.2 ± 0.2 s–1) for SΔTM D614.
source: ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the RBD-down to the RBD-up transition (kup = 2.2 ± 0.2 s–1) but reduced the RBD-up to RBD-down transition to kdown = 1.3 ± 0.1 s–1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ACE2 binding reduced the RBD-up to RBD-down transition to kdown = 1.3 ± 0.1 s–1 for SΔTM D614.
source: ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the RBD-down to the RBD-up transition (kup = 2.2 ± 0.2 s–1) but reduced the RBD-up to RBD-down transition to kdown = 1.3 ± 0.1 s–1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The effect of ACE2 binding is to capture and stabilize the RBD-up conformation and reduce transitions to the RBD-down conformation.
source: This analysis thus specified that the effect of ACE2 binding is to capture and stabilize the RBD-up conformation and reduce transitions to the RBD-down conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: ACE2 binding does not significantly affect the stability of the down conformation, nor induce transitions to the up conformation.
source: ACE2 binding does not significantly affect the stability of the down conformation, nor induce transitions to the up conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The unbound SΔTM D614G displayed greater occupancy in the RBD-up conformation (59% ± 3%).
source: However, the unbound SΔTM D614G displayed greater occupancy in the RBD-up conformation (59% ± 3%), and the overall level of dynamics was reduced as compared to D614 (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: The overall level of dynamics was reduced for SΔTM D614G as compared to D614.
source: However, the unbound SΔTM D614G displayed greater occupancy in the RBD-up conformation (59% ± 3%), and the overall level of dynamics was reduced as compared to D614 (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is observed in the TDPs shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: For unbound SΔTM D614G, the rate constants kup and kdown were reduced to 2.0 ± 0.2 and 1.6 ± 0.2 s–1, respectively.
source: The rate constants, kup and kdown, were reduced to 2.0 ± 0.2 and 1.6 ± 0.2 s–1, respectively (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: ACE2 binding further increased the RBD-up occupancy to 69% ± 4% for SΔTM D614G.
source: ACE2 binding further increased the RBD-up occupancy to 69% ± 4% and reduced the overall level of dynamics shown in the TDPs (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: For SΔTM D614G, ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the rate of transition from the RBD-down to the RBD-up conformation (kup = 2.0 ± 0.4 s–1).
source: As seen for D614, ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the rate of transition from the RBD-down to the RBD-up conformation (kup = 2.0 ± 0.4 s–1) but reduced the rate of transition to the RBD-down conformation to kdown = 0.7 ± 0.1 s–1 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: For SΔTM D614G, ACE2 binding reduced the rate of transition to the RBD-down conformation to kdown = 0.7 ± 0.1 s–1.
source: As seen for D614, ACE2 binding had minimal effect on the rate of transition from the RBD-down to the RBD-up conformation (kup = 2.0 ± 0.4 s–1) but reduced the rate of transition to the RBD-down conformation to kdown = 0.7 ± 0.1 s–1 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The D614G mutation shifted the conformational equilibrium in favor of the RBD-up conformation.
source: Thus, consistent with structural studies (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a), the D614G mutation shifted the conformational equilibrium in favor of the RBD-up conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data and is consistent with cited structural studies.

claim: ACE2 binding stabilized the RBD-up conformation without affecting the energetics of the RBD-down conformation for both D614 and D614G.
source: Also, here again, ACE2 binding stabilized the RBD-up conformation without affecting the energetics of the RBD-down conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: Imaging SΔTM pre-incubated with RBD-directed mAbs revealed a predominant low-FRET state associated with the RBD-up conformation.
source: Imaging SΔTM pre-incubated with each of the above mAbs revealed a predominant low-FRET state associated with the RBD-up conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in smFRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RBD-directed mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614 as compared to the unbound spike, although none to the extent seen for ACE2.
source: In all cases, the mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614 as compared to the unbound spike, although none to the extent seen for ACE2 (Figure 4A); and the effect of REGN10987 and S309 did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The effect of REGN10987 and S309 on stabilizing the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614 did not reach statistical significance.
source: In all cases, the mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614 as compared to the unbound spike, although none to the extent seen for ACE2 (Figure 4A); and the effect of REGN10987 and S309 did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is determined from statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The RBD-directed mAbs generally induced a larger effect on the rate of transition from the RBD-up to the RBD-down conformation (kdown), with a minor effect on the reverse transition (kup).
source: As observed during ACE2 binding, the mAbs generally induced a larger effect on the rate of transition from the RBD-up to the RBD-down conformation (kdown), with a minor effect on the reverse transition (kup; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: None of the RBD-directed mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation for SΔTM D614G to a significant extent.
source: In contrast, none of the mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation for SΔTM D614G to a significant extent (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that the effect of the D614G mutation is sufficient to enable mAb binding without further conformational changes.
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The effect of the D614G mutation is sufficient to enable mAb binding without further conformational changes.
source: In contrast, none of the mAbs stabilized the RBD-up conformation for SΔTM D614G to a significant extent (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that the effect of the D614G mutation is sufficient to enable mAb binding without further conformational changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mAbs do not further stabilize the RBD-up conformation of D614G.

claim: 4A8 treatment of SΔTM D614 stabilized the low-FRET state to a comparable extent as seen for the RBD-targeted mAbs, although the effect did not reach statistical significance.
source: 4A8 treatment of SΔTM D614 stabilized the low-FRET state to a comparable extent as seen for the RBD-targeted mAbs, although the effect did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The stalk-directed mAbs 1A9 and 2G12 significantly stabilized the RBD-up conformation of SΔTM D614.
source: The stalk-directed mAbs 1A9 and 2G12 significantly stabilized the RBD-up conformation (Figure 4A), although kinetic analysis revealed a modulation of the dynamics that was distinct from the S1-targeted mAbs.
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For SΔTM D614, the stalk-directed mAbs 1A9 and 2G12 reduced kdown while increasing kup.
source: Here, in both cases kdown was reduced, while kup was increased (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For SΔTM D614G, 4A8 had only a minor effect on RBD-up occupancy or kinetics.
source: For SΔTM D614G, 4A8 had only a minor effect on RBD-up occupancy or kinetics, again suggesting that the mAb binds without affecting the conformational equilibrium (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs stabilized RBD-up for SΔTM D614G, though not to a statistically significant extent.
source: However, the stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs stabilized RBD-up, though not to a statistically significant extent, and induced increases in kup (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is determined from HMM analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs induced increases in kup for SΔTM D614G.
source: However, the stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs stabilized RBD-up, though not to a statistically significant extent, and induced increases in kup (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The S2 stalk-targeting mAbs allosterically induce transition of the RDB to the up conformation on both the D614 and D614G spikes.
source: These data indicate that the S2 stalk-targeting mAbs studied here allosterically induce transition of the RDB to the up conformation on both the D614 and D614G spikes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The RBD- and NTD-targeting mAbs capture the up conformation without actively inducing a conformational change, similar to the effects of ACE2 on the RBD conformation.
source: In contrast, the RBD- and NTD-targeting mAbs studied here capture the up conformation without actively inducing a conformational change, similar to the effects of ACE2 on the RBD conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: Incubation of SΔTM D614 or D614G with MAb362IgA1 or REGN10987 resulted in statistically significant reductions in ACE2 binding.
source: Incubation of SΔTM D614 or D614G with MAb362IgA1 or REGN10987 resulted in statistically significant reductions in ACE2 binding that are consistent with previous reports at comparable concentrations (Ejemel et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2020; Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is determined from FCS experiments shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: mAbs that stabilized the RBD-up conformation without blocking the ACE2-binding site tended to promote ACE2 binding.
source: Overall, mAbs that stabilized the RBD-up conformation without blocking the ACE2-binding site tended to promote ACE2 binding (Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed in FCS data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a very strong correlation (rs = 0.9048) between ACE2 binding and modulation of the SΔTM RBD conformational equilibrium across all the mAbs under consideration.
source: Calculation of the Spearman coefficient indicated a very strong correlation (rs = 0.9048) between ACE2 binding and modulation of the SΔTM RBD conformational equilibrium across all the mAbs under consideration (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is determined from statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: S309 and 4A8 provided a slight enhancement of ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614.
source: S309 and 4A8 provided a slight enhancement of ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614, consistent with their modest impacts on RBD conformation.
evidence: This is observed in FCS data and is consistent with smFRET data.

claim: S309 had no significant effect on ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614G.
source: In contrast, S309 had no significant effect on ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614G, and 4A8 had a slight inhibition of ACE2 binding, again consistent with their modulation of RBD conformation.
evidence: This is observed in FCS data and is consistent with smFRET data.

claim: 4A8 had a slight inhibition of ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614G.
source: In contrast, S309 had no significant effect on ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614G, and 4A8 had a slight inhibition of ACE2 binding, again consistent with their modulation of RBD conformation.
evidence: This is observed in FCS data and is consistent with smFRET data.

claim: The stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs induced the greatest enhancement of ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614 and D614G.
source: Of note, the stalk-targeting 1A9 and 2G12 mAbs induced the greatest enhancement of ACE2 binding to SΔTM D614 and D614G, consistent with their allosteric modulation of RBD conformation.
evidence: This is observed in FCS data and is consistent with smFRET data.

claim: ACE2 stabilizes the RBD in the up conformation, which is a conformation that pre-exists prior to ACE2 binding.
source: Our analysis of S conformational dynamics shows that ACE2 stabilizes the RBD in the up conformation, which, in agreement with structural data, is a conformation that pre-exists prior to ACE2 binding (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data and is consistent with cited structural data.

claim: ACE2 binding does not affect the rate of transition to the RBD-up conformation.
source: Determination of the kinetics of conformational changes through HMM analysis indicated that ACE2 binding does not affect the rate of transition to the RBD-up conformation.
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis.

claim: ACE2 captures the RBD-up conformation and reduces the rate of transition to the RBD-down conformation.
source: Instead, ACE2 captures the RBD-up conformation and reduces the rate of transition to the RBD-down conformation.
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis.

claim: ACE2 binding to S occurs through the capture of a pre-existing conformation rather than inducing a conformational change.
source: This analysis of S dynamics specifies that ACE2 binding to S does not induce a conformational change in S, but rather occurs through the capture of a pre-existing conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The intrinsic dynamics of S control the rate or efficiency of membrane fusion during virus entry.
source: As ACE2 binding is an essential step during SARS-CoV-2 entry, our interpretation implicates the intrinsic dynamics of S in controlling the rate or efficiency of membrane fusion during virus entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of ACE2 binding in virus entry.

claim: Factors that stabilize the RBD-up conformation would likely increase the rate of membrane fusion.
source: Accordingly, factors that stabilize the RBD-up conformation would likely increase the rate of membrane fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of the RBD-up conformation in membrane fusion.

claim: The D614G mutation stabilized the RBD-up conformation, which likely relates to how the mutation enhances infectivity.
source: Our data demonstrate that the D614G mutation stabilized the RBD-up conformation, consistent with previous reports, which likely relates to how the mutation enhances infectivity (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFRET data and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: D614G does not increase the rate of ACE2 binding to S.
source: Previous studies have shown that D614G does not increase the rate of ACE2 binding to S (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a), as might be expected for a conformational capture-binding mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Further rearrangements in the RBD, perhaps localized in the RBM, may be necessary to fully engage ACE2 beyond transition to the up conformation.
source: This may indicate that further rearrangements in the RBD, perhaps localized in the RBM, are necessary to fully engage ACE2 beyond transition to the up conformation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that D614G does not increase the rate of ACE2 binding.

claim: Analysis of the dynamics of the unbound D614G variant showed an overall reduction in dynamics as compared to D614, consistent with the increased thermostability of the S trimer with the D614G mutation.
source: Analysis of the dynamics of the unbound D614G variant showed an overall reduction in dynamics as compared to D614, consistent with the increased thermostability of the S trimer with the D614G mutation (Zhang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data and is consistent with cited structural studies.

claim: The predominant effect of the D614G mutation was the reduction of the rate of transition to the down conformation.
source: Like ACE2 binding to the D614 spike, the predominant effect of the D614G mutation was the reduction of the rate of transition to the down conformation.
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis.

claim: The D614G mutation increases the activation energy for transition to the down conformation, which is mainly explained by an increase in thermodynamic stability of the RBD-up conformation.
source: This observation indicates an increase in the activation energy, which is mainly explained by an increase in thermodynamic stability of the RBD-up conformation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis and is illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: ACE2 binding to S D614G had an additive effect on the RBD position, pushing the equilibrium further toward the up conformation than either ACE2 binding or the D614G mutation did independently.
source: ACE2 binding to S D614G had an additive effect on the RBD position, pushing the equilibrium further toward the up conformation than either ACE2 binding or the D614G mutation did independently.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data.

claim: The D614G mutation permits further stabilization of an intermediate conformation captured by ACE2 binding.
source: Thus, the D614G mutation permits further stabilization of an intermediate conformation captured by ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect of D614G and ACE2 binding.

claim: Residue D614 forms a salt bridge with K854 in the fusion-peptide proximal region, which is lost with the D614G mutation.
source: Residue D614 is distal to the RBD and forms a salt bridge with K854 in the fusion-peptide proximal region, which is lost with the D614G mutation (Xiong et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Zhou et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The D614-K854 electrostatic interaction had a destabilizing effect on the thermodynamics of the RBD-up conformation.
source: Our analysis shows that the D614-K854 electrostatic interaction had a destabilizing effect on the thermodynamics of the RBD-up conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of the D614G mutation on RBD conformation.

claim: The D614G mutation provides a fitness advantage by mimicking the effects of receptor binding.
source: The similar impacts of D614G and ACE2 binding on the S energetic landscape imply that the mutation provides a fitness advantage by mimicking the effects of receptor binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of D614G and ACE2 binding on RBD conformation.

claim: A long-range allosteric connection exists between the RBD and the region surrounding the fusion peptide.
source: Such a long-range allosteric connection between the RBD and the region surrounding the fusion peptide has been reported for influenza hemagglutinin and the Ebola virus envelope glycoprotein (Das et al., 2018; Das et al., 2020; Yewdell et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other viral fusion proteins.

claim: There is a common mechanistic connection between receptor binding and triggering movement of the fusion peptide (or fusion loop) among class-I viral fusion proteins.
source: This suggests a common mechanistic connection between receptor binding and triggering movement of the fusion peptide (or fusion loop) among class-I viral fusion proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the allosteric connection observed in SARS-CoV-2 S and other viral fusion proteins.

claim: mAbs that target S1 of the D614 spike have a similar impact on conformational dynamics as ACE2, with the predominant effect being the reduction in the rate of transition to the down conformation.
source: We find that mAbs that target S1 of the D614 spike, including the RBD and NTD, have a similar impact on conformational dynamics as ACE2, with the predominant effect being the reduction in the rate of transition to the down conformation.
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis.

claim: The overall minimal effect of S1-targeting mAbs on the rate of transition to the up conformation is consistent with thermodynamic stabilization and the capture of a pre-existing S conformation.
source: The overall minimal effect on the rate of transition to the up conformation is again consistent with thermodynamic stabilization and the capture of a pre-existing S conformation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis and is illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: mAb S309 had a notably modest effect on the stability of the up conformation, consistent with structural data demonstrating that it binds to the RBD in either the up or down positions.
source: mAb S309 had a notably modest effect on the stability of the up conformation, consistent with structural data demonstrating that it binds to the RBD in either the up or down positions (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data and is consistent with cited structural data.

claim: RBD- and NTD-targeting mAbs had minimal effect on the conformation of the D614G spike.
source: Overall, RBD- and NTD-targeting mAbs had minimal effect on the conformation of the D614G spike.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data.

claim: mAb S309 modestly destabilized the RBD-up conformation of the D614G spike.
source: Of note, mAb S309 modestly destabilized the RBD-up conformation.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET data.

claim: The mechanism of broad neutralization by S309 remains unclear, but its modulation of the RBD position likely plays some role and may impact downstream conformational changes related to membrane fusion.
source: As S309 does not prevent ACE2 binding, its mechanism of broad neutralization remains unclear (McCallum et al., 2021a; Pinto et al., 2020). However, its modulation of the RBD position likely plays some role and may impact downstream conformational changes related to membrane fusion.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed modulation of RBD conformation by S309.

claim: The S2-targeted mAbs induce conformational changes in the RBD by reducing the activation energy for transition into the up conformation, while also stabilizing the up conformation.
source: Our kinetic analyses have shown that the S1-targeted ligands considered here capture the RBD-up conformation. In contrast, the S2-targeted mAbs considered here induce conformational changes in the RBD by reducing the activation energy for transition into the up conformation, while also stabilizing the up conformation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis and is illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography of SARS-CoV-2 virions has revealed the presence of three flexible hinges within the S stalk: the hip, knee, and ankle.
source: Cryo-electron tomography of SARS-CoV-2 virions has revealed the presence of three flexible hinges within the S stalk: the hip, knee, and ankle. These hinges connect the head, and the upper and lower legs of S, and confer flexibility of the spikes (Ke et al., 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-ET studies.

claim: Stalk-targeted mAbs 1A9 and 2G12 allosterically modulate the position of the RBD, enhancing ACE2 binding.
source: Our smFRET data demonstrate that stalk-targeted mAbs 1A9 and 2G12 allosterically modulate the position of the RBD, enhancing ACE2 binding.
evidence: This is observed in the smFRET and FCS data.

claim: mAb 1A9 binds an epitope on S in the upper leg of the stalk near the hip and upstream of the heptad repeat two helix.
source: mAb 1A9, which neutralizes SARS-CoV, binds an epitope on S in the upper leg of the stalk near the hip and upstream of the heptad repeat two helix (Lip et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: High sequence conservation in the 1A9 epitope suggests a similar binding site in SARS-CoV-2 S and mode of action in preventing viral membrane fusion.
source: High sequence conservation in the 1A9 epitope suggests a similar binding site in SARS-CoV-2 S and mode of action in preventing viral membrane fusion (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference from sequence conservation.

claim: The stalk epitope recognized by mAb 2G12 is located near the hip and is comprised entirely of glycans.
source: The stalk epitope recognized by mAb 2G12, which does not neutralize SARS-CoV-2, is located near the hip and is comprised entirely of glycans (Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The hip hinge is a critical center for allosteric control of the RBD position.
source: Taken together, our data on 1A9 and 2G12 implicate the hip hinge as a critical center for allosteric control of the RBD position.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of 1A9 and 2G12 on RBD conformation.

claim: mAb CV3-25 binds an epitope in the upper leg of the stalk near the knee.
source: Further support for the existence of allosteric centers in S2 came from other smFRET analyses of mAb CV3-25 (Jennewein et al., 2021), which binds an epitope in the upper leg of the stalk near the knee (Li et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CV3-25 was found to promote the RBD-up conformation.
source: CV3-25 was also found to promote the RBD-up conformation (Li et al., 2022b; Ullah et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Enhancement of neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 was observed with the simultaneous use of S309 and S2E12.
source: Similarly, enhancement of neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 was observed with the simultaneous use of S309 and S2E12 (Starr and Czudnochowski, 2021; Tortorici et al., 2020) which targets the RBM.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The synergy in neutralization from S309 and S2E12 likely stems from the combined effect of S309 on S conformation and blocking ACE2 binding by S2E12.
source: This likely stems from the combined effect of S309 on S conformation and blocking ACE2 binding by S2E12.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms of action of S309 and S2E12.

claim: Similar synergy in neutralization might come from the combination of 4A8 with RBM-directed mAbs.
source: Our results suggest that similar synergy in neutralization might come from the combination of 4A8 with RBM-directed mAbs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the effects of 4A8 on RBD conformation and ACE2 binding.

claim: The promotion of the RBD-up conformation by NTD-directed mAbs like 4A8, or stalk-directed mAbs like 1A9 and 2G12, presents a strategy for enhancement of neutralization through combination therapies with RBM-directed mAbs.
source: The promotion of the RBD-up conformation, which exposes the ACE2-binding site, by NTD-directed mAbs like 4A8, or stalk-directed mAbs like 1A9 and 2G12, presents a strategy for enhancement of neutralization through combination therapies with RBM-directed mAbs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results suggest the potential for synergistic inhibition of virus entry and increased potency through the combination of mAbs that target diverse epitopes.
source: The results presented here suggest the potential for synergistic inhibition of virus entry and increased potency through the combination of mAbs that target diverse epitopes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
